concepts.topicTitle: Physical Properties of Metals, Non-metals, and Their Exceptions
concepts.label: Lustre, Hardness, Malleability and Ductility of Metals
concepts.cardText: Metals, in their pure state, have a shining surface; this property is called metallic lustre. Metals are generally hard, though the hardness varies from metal to metal. Some metals can be beaten into thin sheets, a property called malleability, and gold and silver are the most malleable metals. The ability of metals to be drawn into thin wires is called ductility. Gold is the most ductile metal: a wire of about 2 km length can be drawn from one gram of gold. It is because of their malleability and ductility that metals can be given different shapes according to our needs.

concepts.topicTitle: Physical Properties of Metals, Non-metals, and Their Exceptions
concepts.label: Metals as Conductors of Heat and Electricity and Their Sonority
concepts.cardText: Metals are good conductors of heat and have high melting points; the best conductors of heat are silver and copper, while lead and mercury are comparatively poor conductors. This is why metals are used to make cooking vessels. Metals also conduct electricity, which is why wires that carry current in homes have a coating of polyvinylchloride (PVC) or a rubber-like material around the metal. Metals that produce a sound on striking a hard surface are said to be sonorous, so school bells are made of metals. In summary, metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity, and they are solids at room temperature except mercury, a liquid.

concepts.topicTitle: Physical Properties of Metals, Non-metals, and Their Exceptions
concepts.label: Physical Properties of Non-metals
concepts.cardText: There are very few non-metals as compared to metals. Examples of non-metals are carbon, sulphur, iodine, oxygen and hydrogen. The non-metals are either solids or gases except bromine, which is a liquid. Non-metals have properties opposite to that of metals: they are neither malleable nor ductile, and they are bad conductors of heat and electricity, except graphite, which conducts electricity. Comparing the observations for metals and non-metals shows that we cannot group elements according to their physical properties alone, as there are many exceptions.

concepts.topicTitle: Physical Properties of Metals, Non-metals, and Their Exceptions
concepts.label: Exceptions in the Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
concepts.cardText: Physical properties alone cannot classify elements because of exceptions. All metals except mercury exist as solids at room temperature. Metals have high melting points but gallium and caesium have very low melting points and will melt if kept on the palm. Iodine is a non-metal but it is lustrous. Carbon is a non-metal that can exist in different forms, each called an allotrope. Diamond, an allotrope of carbon, is the hardest natural substance known with a very high melting and boiling point, and graphite, another allotrope, is a conductor of electricity. Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) are so soft that they can be cut with a knife, and they have low densities and low melting points.

concepts.topicTitle: Chemical Reactivity of Metals with Oxygen and Amphoteric Oxides
concepts.label: Reaction of Metals with Oxygen
concepts.cardText: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides: metal + oxygen gives metal oxide. When copper is heated in air it combines with oxygen to form copper(II) oxide, a black oxide, and aluminium forms aluminium oxide. Metals do not all react with oxygen at the same rate; they show different reactivities towards oxygen. Potassium and sodium react so vigorously that they catch fire if kept in the open, so they are kept immersed in kerosene oil. At ordinary temperature the surfaces of magnesium, aluminium, zinc and lead are covered with a thin layer of oxide that prevents further oxidation. Iron filings burn vigorously in a flame, copper does not burn but gets a black copper(II) oxide layer, and silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.

concepts.topicTitle: Chemical Reactivity of Metals with Oxygen and Amphoteric Oxides
concepts.label: Basic, Amphoteric and Water-Soluble Metal Oxides
concepts.cardText: Most metals give rise to basic oxides, while most non-metals produce acidic oxides when dissolved in water. But some metal oxides, such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide, show both acidic and basic behaviour. Metal oxides that react with both acids and bases to produce salts and water are known as amphoteric oxides. Aluminium oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to give aluminium chloride and water, and with sodium hydroxide to give sodium aluminate and water. Most metal oxides are insoluble in water, but some dissolve in water to form alkalis; sodium oxide and potassium oxide give sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide.

concepts.topicTitle: Chemical Reactions of Metals with Water and Steam
concepts.label: Reaction of Metals with Water and Steam
concepts.cardText: Metals react with water and produce a metal oxide and hydrogen gas; metal oxides that are soluble in water dissolve in it to further form metal hydroxide. But all metals do not react with water. Potassium and sodium react violently with cold water: the reaction is so violent and exothermic that the evolved hydrogen immediately catches fire. The reaction of calcium with water is less violent, the heat is not enough for the hydrogen to catch fire, and calcium starts floating because bubbles of hydrogen stick to it. Magnesium does not react with cold water but reacts with hot water to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen. Aluminium, iron and zinc do not react with cold or hot water, but react with steam to form the metal oxide and hydrogen. Lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water at all.

concepts.cardText: Metals react with acids to give a salt and hydrogen gas, but not all in the same manner. In the test with dilute hydrochloric acid the rate of formation of bubbles is fastest with magnesium and the reaction is also the most exothermic. The reactivity decreases in the order Mg > Al > Zn > Fe. With copper no bubbles are seen and the temperature stays unchanged, showing that copper does not react with dilute HCl. Metals above hydrogen in the activity series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Hydrogen gas is not evolved when a metal reacts with nitric acid, because HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises the H2 produced to water and itself gets reduced to nitrogen oxides. But magnesium and manganese react with very dilute HNO3 to evolve H2 gas.

concepts.topicTitle: The Reactivity Series and Displacement Reactions
concepts.label: Displacement Reactions and the Reactivity Series
concepts.cardText: Reactive metals can displace less reactive metals from their compounds in solution or molten form. Displacement reactions give better evidence about the reactivity of metals than their reactions with oxygen, water and acids, because not all metals react with these reagents. If metal A displaces metal B from its solution, it is more reactive than B: metal A + salt solution of B gives salt solution of A + metal B. In Activity 3.12 the iron nail in copper sulphate solution shows that iron is more reactive than copper. The reactivity series, or activity series, is a list of metals arranged in the order of their decreasing activities, from potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron and lead through copper, mercury and silver to gold, the least reactive.

concepts.topicTitle: Formation and Chemical Nature of Ionic Compounds
concepts.label: Why Elements React: Attaining a Filled Valence Shell
concepts.cardText: Noble gases, which have a completely filled valence shell, show little chemical activity. We therefore explain the reactivity of elements as a tendency to attain a completely filled valence shell. A sodium atom has one electron in its outermost shell. If it loses that electron from its M shell, its L shell becomes the outermost shell with a stable octet. The nucleus still has 11 protons but the electrons number 10, so there is a net positive charge, giving a sodium cation Na+. Chlorine has seven electrons in its outermost shell and requires one more to complete its octet. After gaining an electron the chlorine atom gets a unit negative charge, giving a chloride anion Cl-. Metals can form positive ions by losing electrons to non-metals, and non-metals form negatively charged ions by gaining electrons.

concepts.topicTitle: Formation and Chemical Nature of Ionic Compounds
concepts.label: Ionic (Electrovalent) Compounds
concepts.cardText: If sodium and chlorine react, the electron lost by sodium is taken up by chlorine, so the two elements have a give-and-take relation. Sodium and chloride ions, being oppositely charged, attract each other and are held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction to exist as sodium chloride (NaCl). Sodium chloride does not exist as molecules but as aggregates of oppositely charged ions. In magnesium chloride, a magnesium atom loses two electrons to become Mg2+, and two chlorine atoms each gain one electron. The compounds formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal are known as ionic compounds or electrovalent compounds.

concepts.topicTitle: Physical Properties of Ionic Compounds
concepts.label: Physical Properties of Ionic Compounds
concepts.cardText: Ionic compounds are solids and are somewhat hard because of the strong force of attraction between the positive and negative ions; they are generally brittle and break into pieces when pressure is applied. They have high melting and boiling points because a considerable amount of energy is required to break the strong inter-ionic attraction. Electrovalent compounds are generally soluble in water and insoluble in solvents such as kerosene and petrol. A solution of an ionic compound in water contains ions, which move to the opposite electrodes when electricity is passed, so it conducts electricity. In the solid state they do not conduct electricity because movement of ions in the rigid structure is not possible, but in the molten state the electrostatic forces are overcome by heat and the ions move freely and conduct electricity.

concepts.topicTitle: Extraction of Metals (Metallurgy): Roasting, Calcination, and Reduction
concepts.label: Occurrence of Metals: Minerals, Ores and the Activity Series
concepts.cardText: The earth's crust is the major source of metals, and seawater also contains some soluble salts such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride. The elements or compounds which occur naturally in the earth's crust are known as minerals. At some places minerals contain a very high percentage of a particular metal and the metal can be profitably extracted from it; these minerals are called ores. The metals at the bottom of the activity series are least reactive and are often found in a free state, such as gold, silver, platinum and copper. The metals at the top (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are so reactive that they are never found free in nature. The metals in the middle (Zn, Fe, Pb) are moderately reactive and found mainly as oxides, sulphides or carbonates. So metals are grouped into those of low, medium and high reactivity.

concepts.topicTitle: Extraction of Metals (Metallurgy): Roasting, Calcination, and Reduction
concepts.label: Extracting Metals Low in the Activity Series
concepts.cardText: Metals low in the activity series are very unreactive, and the oxides of these metals can be reduced to metals by heating alone. Cinnabar (HgS) is an ore of mercury. When it is heated in air it is first converted into mercuric oxide (HgO), and mercuric oxide is then reduced to mercury on further heating. Similarly, copper which is found as Cu2S in nature can be obtained from its ore by just heating in air.

concepts.topicTitle: Extraction of Metals (Metallurgy): Roasting, Calcination, and Reduction
concepts.label: Extracting Metals in the Middle of the Activity Series: Roasting, Calcination and Reduction
concepts.cardText: Metals in the middle of the activity series such as iron, zinc, lead and copper are moderately reactive, and are usually present as sulphides or carbonates in nature. It is easier to obtain a metal from its oxide than from its sulphide or carbonate, so prior to reduction the sulphides and carbonates must be converted into metal oxides. The sulphide ores are converted into oxides by heating strongly in the presence of excess air, a process known as roasting. The carbonate ores are changed into oxides by heating strongly in limited air, a process known as calcination. The metal oxides are then reduced to the metals by suitable reducing agents such as carbon; for example, zinc oxide heated with carbon gives metallic zinc. Obtaining metals from their compounds is a reduction process.

concepts.topicTitle: Extraction of Metals (Metallurgy): Roasting, Calcination, and Reduction
concepts.label: The Thermit Reaction: Reducing Oxides by Displacement
concepts.cardText: Besides using carbon (coke) to reduce metal oxides to metals, displacement reactions can also be used. Highly reactive metals such as sodium, calcium and aluminium are used as reducing agents because they can displace metals of lower reactivity from their compounds. For example, heating manganese dioxide with aluminium powder gives molten manganese and aluminium oxide. These displacement reactions are highly exothermic: the heat evolved is so large that the metals are produced in the molten state. The reaction of iron(III) oxide with aluminium is used to join railway tracks or cracked machine parts, and is known as the thermit reaction.

concepts.topicTitle: Extraction of Metals (Metallurgy): Roasting, Calcination, and Reduction
concepts.label: Extracting Metals at the Top of the Activity Series: Electrolytic Reduction
concepts.cardText: The metals high up in the reactivity series are very reactive and cannot be obtained from their compounds by heating with carbon. For example, carbon cannot reduce the oxides of sodium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium to the metals, because these metals have more affinity for oxygen than carbon. These metals are obtained by electrolytic reduction. Sodium, magnesium and calcium are obtained by the electrolysis of their molten chlorides: the metals are deposited at the cathode, the negatively charged electrode, while chlorine is liberated at the anode, the positively charged electrode. Similarly, aluminium is obtained by the electrolytic reduction of aluminium oxide.

concepts.topicTitle: Electrolytic Refining of Metals
concepts.label: Electrolytic Refining
concepts.cardText: The metals produced by the various reduction processes are not very pure. They contain impurities, which must be removed to obtain pure metals. The most widely used method for refining impure metals is electrolytic refining. Many metals, such as copper, zinc, tin, nickel, silver and gold, are refined electrolytically. In this process the impure metal is made the anode and a thin strip of pure metal is made the cathode. A solution of the metal salt is used as an electrolyte. On passing current, the pure metal from the anode dissolves into the electrolyte and an equivalent amount of pure metal from the electrolyte is deposited on the cathode. The soluble impurities go into the solution, whereas the insoluble impurities settle down at the bottom of the anode and are known as anode mud.

concepts.topicTitle: Corrosion and Prevention through Galvanisation and Alloying
concepts.label: Corrosion and the Conditions for Rusting
concepts.cardText: Silver articles become black after some time when exposed to air because silver reacts with sulphur in the air to form a coating of silver sulphide. Copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air and slowly loses its shiny brown surface and gains a green coat of basic copper carbonate. Iron, when exposed to moist air for a long time, acquires a coating of a brown flaky substance called rust. In the activity with three test tubes, iron nails rust in test tube A, where they are exposed to both air and water, but do not rust in B, where there is only water without dissolved air, or in C, where the air is dry. So iron rusts in the presence of both air and water. The surface of some metals, such as iron, is corroded when exposed to moist air for a long period; this phenomenon is known as corrosion.

concepts.topicTitle: Corrosion and Prevention through Galvanisation and Alloying
concepts.label: Prevention of Corrosion and Galvanisation
concepts.cardText: The rusting of iron can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising or making alloys. Galvanisation is a method of protecting steel and iron from rusting by coating them with a thin layer of zinc. The galvanised article is protected against rusting even if the zinc coating is broken, because zinc is more reactive than iron and is attacked first.

concepts.topicTitle: Corrosion and Prevention through Galvanisation and Alloying
concepts.label: Alloys
concepts.cardText: Alloying is a very good method of improving the properties of a metal. Iron is the most widely used metal but is never used in its pure state, because pure iron is very soft and stretches easily when hot. If it is mixed with a small amount of carbon (about 0.05 %), it becomes hard and strong, and when iron is mixed with nickel and chromium we get stainless steel, which is hard and does not rust. An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, prepared by first melting the primary metal and then dissolving the other elements in it in definite proportions, then cooling. If one of the metals is mercury, the alloy is an amalgam. The electrical conductivity and melting point of an alloy is less than that of pure metals: brass and bronze are not good conductors, and solder, an alloy of lead and tin, has a low melting point and is used to weld electrical wires. Pure 24 carat gold is very soft, so it is alloyed with silver or copper; 22 carat gold has 22 parts pure gold to 2 parts of copper or silver.
